figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of the pretraining framework. (a) Imagereport pairs with optional clinical context. (b) Heatmaptranscript pairs capturing physicians’ visual attention. (c-d) Comparison between existing methods and ours. (e) Imagetext retrieval results on the MIMIC-5x200 dataset [91]. Clinical context and gaze data are available for a subset of cases. “TS” denotes transcript.
Figure 5: Comparison of supervised classification performance in terms of AUROC on the Shenzhen [21] dataset.
Table 4: Zero-shot classification performance (%) on RSNA [56] and Shenzhen [21] dataset. Since CheXWorld [78] lacks a text encoder, its results are omitted (Best, Second Best).

Figure A15: Ablation study on the impact of hyperparameters 𝜆 and 𝜌 across classification (AUROC), segmentation (Dice), and retrieval (P@K) tasks on multiple datasets. The retrieval task is conducted on the MIMIC-5x200 [26, 91] dataset. Our CoGaze achieves optimal performance at 𝜆 = 0.8 and 𝜌 = 0.25.
Table 5: Segmentation performance (%) on the RSNA [56] and TBX11K [42] dataset (Best, Second Best).

Table 6: Ablation study on supervision strategies, context integration, and gaze ratio for the MIMIC-CXR report generation task. “BS” and “CC” denotes BERTScore [83] and clinical context, respectively. 𝑛Mi-F1 and 𝑛Ma-F1 refer to the micro- and macro-F1 scores computed by CheXbert, with 𝑛 observations. Higher is better for all metrics.

Figure A14: Examples of structured radiology reports generated by CoGaze (Llama-3B). Correctly generated words are highlighted in green, while acceptable words are highlighted in orange. Incorrect or missing findings are underlined in red.
Figure 2: (A) Overview of our CoGaze. (B) Context-infused vision encoder. Gaze supervision is used only during pretraining.
Figure A12: Attention visualizations of CoGaze, CoGaze w/o Gaze, and CoGaze w/o Context on pneumothorax (SIIM [80]) and tuberculosis (Shenzhen [21]) cases.

Figure A13: Examples of free-text radiology reports generated by PromptMRG [25], MLRG [39], and CoGaze (DistilGPT2). Words in the generated reports that match the reference are highlighted in the same color. Greater color diversity reflects broader coverage of clinical findings, while longer color spans suggest more detailed descriptions. Incorrect predictions are underlined.

Figure 7: Qualitative results. (A) Free-text radiology reports generated from PromptMRG [25], MLRG [39], and CoGaze (DistilGPT2). (B-C) Attention maps of CoGaze, CoGaze w/o Gaze, and CoGaze w/o Context on pneumothorax and tuberculosis cases. (D) Comparison between radiologist’ annotations and CoGaze-predicted heatmaps.
Table A13: Comparison between context-based method and CoGaze in supervised classification (CLS) and segmentation (SEG) performance.
Figure A11: Comparison between radiologists’ annotations and CoGaze-predicted heatmaps on the MIMIC-CXR dataset (Appendix Tab. A9).

Table 1: Free-text report generation on MIMIC-CXR [26] dataset. △ denotes CoGaze’s gain over the strongest baseline. EGMA [45] is reproduced using its official code with DistilGPT2, while other results are from original papers (Best, Second Best).
